author: Codex assessment agent /root/libertarian_historical (AI-assisted)
changeNote: Completed each of the 240 current questions as an interpreted representative doctrine, with question-specific reasoning, source references and explicit conditional neutral modelling. Separate review pending. No 12Axes answer or score imported.

metadata.name: Nazism (German National Socialism, 1920–1945)
metadata.description: German National Socialism, 1920–1945: racial exclusion, dictatorship, expansionist war and an economy subordinated to rearmament. All racial claims are descriptions of the ideology’s false doctrines, not scientific findings.
metadata.scope: The NSDAP programme, Hitler’s 1936 economic memorandum and documented regime practice, interpreted through Holocaust scholarship. Programme rhetoric is distinguished from later private ownership under compulsory state direction. Membership and welfare were racially exclusionary; apparent social provisions are not presented as universal rights. This is a historical doctrine with no claimed incumbent exemplar. Modern technology answers are conditional analogies, not invented historical pronouncements. Racial causation answers describe Nazi assertions and never endorse them.
metadata.phrase: Racially exclusionary dictatorship and expansionist nationalism, with society and economic production subordinated to state power and war.

sources.title: NSDAP programme of 24 February 1920, Nuremberg document 1708-PS
Hitler’s confidential memo on autarky, August 1936
The German Churches and the Nazi State
Reich Citizenship Law and First Regulation, September–November 1935

axes.brief: Leader dictatorship and racial exclusion displace universal suffrage, competitive opposition and independent institutional control.
axes.counterEvidence: The 1920 programme invoked a central parliament and citizen equality within racial restrictions; subsequent dictatorship removed even that limited competitive interpretation.

answers.rationale: The regime’s leadership principle did not make continued authority conditional on competitive electoral defeat or renewal.
Experts served racial and strategic objectives; technical merit did not entitle an independent panel to replace the political leader.

The 1935 regulation reserves voting to full Reich citizens without stating an education or intelligence threshold, while citizenship itself is racially restricted and can be withdrawn by political authorities. Formal participation for a selected citizen body therefore coexists with rejection of an unconditional individual voting right; exclusion of non-citizens alone does not answer this citizen-specific question.
Concentrated leadership could impose national decisions without an independent parliamentary majority’s consent.
Opposition organisations had no equal right to challenge the regime’s monopoly of political authority.
Independent opposition scrutiny of public money was incompatible with the suppression of rival political organisations.
Courts could not hold an independent constitutional veto over supreme leadership’s political objectives.
Worker organisations were subordinate instruments rather than independent selectors of national government.
The programme demanded closure of organisations opposing its core requirements, supporting political exclusion from elections.
A popular right to repeal the leader’s laws would conflict with the dictatorship’s final authority.
The leadership principle concentrates major national policy decisions in the leader rather than plural representative institutions.
An independently enforceable parliamentary removal process contradicts supreme personal political authority.
Electoral scheduling could be subordinated to political leadership rather than independently enforced renewal.
Voter recall would create an autonomous popular authority inconsistent with hierarchical leadership.
Government authority did not require accountability to a competitive electorate or independent elected opposition.
The armed forces were to serve the political leader; a military entitlement to depose that leader on its own judgement would be rejected.

axes.brief: The dictatorship subordinates personal privacy, expression and procedure to racial and political policing.
axes.counterEvidence: Some ordinary liberties could persist for favoured people, but these were conditional privileges rather than equal guarantees. Modern surveillance analogies follow this institutional principle.

answers.rationale: Private adult choice is subordinate to the regime’s racial-health and disciplinary objectives even without immediate harm to others.
Surveillance against serious crime is permissible; requiring a warrant in this example does not conflict with the regime’s broader coercive powers.
Public demonstrations opposing state policy have no protected entitlement to obstruct ordinary activity.
Programme point 23 subjects publications and expression to political-racial censorship rather than protecting offensive criticism.
Programme point 21 assigns compulsory physical-health duties, supporting paternalistic controls for the regime’s population objectives.
Long-term movement tracking would fit comprehensive population and political control in this explicitly modern analogy.
Random intoxication checks are compatible with disciplinary policing and population-health objectives.
Preventive restraint is permissible under the regime’s conception of dangerousness rather than limited to punishment after an offence.
The programme explicitly calls for suppressing cultural works deemed destructive to national life.
Anonymous communication has no independent claim against identification required for political and racial control.
Area-wide threat searches fit the regime’s coercive security model without an individual-suspicion prerequisite.
Political authorities may prohibit gatherings on disorder grounds without treating assembly as a superior individual right.
A universal warrant requirement would restrict the political-policing powers central to the dictatorship.
Publishing confidential official misconduct is not protected when it challenges the regime’s authority or secrecy.
Firearms access is conditional on regime-defined trust and membership, not a general adult self-defence entitlement secured only by violence checks.
Open-ended political-security detention is compatible with the regime’s rejection of independent rights-based judicial restraint.

axes.brief: The programme defines national membership racially and demands cultural subordination, rather than promising inclusion through assimilation alone.
axes.counterEvidence: This is more exclusionary than ordinary civic assimilation: adopting language or customs could not overcome the programme’s false hereditary membership criteria.

answers.rationale: The state privileges the regime-defined German national culture over migrant practices when they conflict.
Separate minority cultural accommodation has no equal public claim within the racial national order.
Those permitted to remain are expected to conform to official national culture, although conformity cannot erase racial exclusion.
Foreign cultural identity cannot claim an equal protected place within the racially defined political community.
Programme point 23 privileges an officially controlled German press and restricts foreign-language political publication.
Minority acknowledgement would depend on its usefulness to the racial national narrative rather than an equal claim based on prior presence.
Public cultural support serves the regime’s predominant national-racial traditions rather than equitable plural funding.
Distinct group identity cannot supersede the imposed unity of the racial national community.
A common public calendar serves uniform national mobilisation rather than equal scheduling for every community.
The programme’s exclusionary conception rejects equal standing for multiple cultural traditions as defining national identity.
State programmes demand participation in the dominant national order, without offering racial outsiders equal membership through participation.
Migrant-language public accommodation is contrary to the regime’s national cultural hierarchy.
Families are expected to transmit the regime’s national and racial identity above autonomous community loyalties.
A minority religious exemption has no independent standing against uniform state restrictions on public appearance.
Several distinct public ways of life are inconsistent with the imposed racial-national community.
Integration policy prioritises national conformity rather than preserving separate community customs.

axes.brief: The 1920 programme demands exclusion and expulsion of racially defined outsiders; usefulness alone does not confer membership.
axes.counterEvidence: Coerced wartime foreign labour is not open immigration or an equal residence right. Admissions for persons treated as German demonstrate why some apparently restrictive universal rules require conditional answers.

answers.rationale: State limits are strongly favoured, although the programme’s racial exclusions are more fundamental than housing-based annual calculations.
Improved living conditions do not establish a settlement right against the programme’s racial admission restrictions.
Skills cannot qualify a racially excluded applicant, while favoured ethnic admission need not depend on skills; a skills-only rule misstates the doctrine.
Reunion may be permitted for favoured members, but permanently settled outsiders have no general equal entitlement to bring relatives.
Refugee need cannot override the regime’s racial criteria for permanent settlement.
Programme point 8 expressly calls for expelling specified non-German immigrants rather than recognising a right to remain.
Employer demand cannot confer a right to permanent admission contrary to racial and national policy.
Domestic provision and the regime-defined national population take priority over economic gains from additional arrivals.
Family entry remains subject to exclusionary state control rather than enjoying a general exemption from admission limits.
A job offer alone cannot override racial membership and security restrictions on entry.
Employer or family sponsorship is neither sufficient for excluded people nor necessary for all favoured ethnic admissions.
Educational qualification by itself cannot supply a residence route independent of the programme’s membership criteria.
Persecution does not confer a right to cross the border against racial exclusion, even where ordinary capacity remains.
Cultural similarity is favoured over diversity, though the ideology’s purported biological ancestry test goes beyond culture alone.
Programme point 7 prioritises citizens and permits expulsion of outsiders when resources are insufficient, opposing equal migrant welfare admission.
Cultural difference is not considered a reason to increase admission within the racial national programme.

axes.brief: Expansion, rearmament and preparation for conquest are central, particularly in the 1936 memorandum.
axes.counterEvidence: Tactical negotiations are possible; they do not make peace or reciprocal disarmament superior to the regime’s territorial and racial objectives.

answers.rationale: The programme’s territorial demands and the 1936 preparations permit aggressive force without a prior attack.
Slower diplomacy is not given priority when it frustrates conquest or strategic opportunity.
The 1936 memorandum demands military preparation despite substantial economic sacrifice.
Strong evidence of an imminent attack would provide ample grounds for force within an already expansionist military doctrine.
Force is not restricted to defence of the state or its allies because territorial conquest is a positive objective.
The programme’s national army and compulsory physical preparation support mass male military obligations.
Avoiding war does not justify concessions that undermine the expansionist national-racial project.
Autonomous weapons are favoured by analogy when they enhance military efficiency, with operational usefulness rather than equal individual rights as the main constraint.
The demand for territory and preparation for expansion require capabilities beyond territorial defence.
Avoiding all war contradicts the programme of violent territorial expansion.
Sustained combat abroad follows directly from preparing the economy and armed forces for conquest.
Leaving territorial claims unresolved is not preferred when leadership considers war an advantageous means to fulfil them.
Threatening force is compatible with coercive pursuit of territorial and strategic concessions.
The doctrine prioritises demonstrated power and strategic expansion over reducing war risk when those aims conflict.
Espionage that improves military advantage is consistent with the overriding war-preparation objective despite diplomatic risks.
Substantial capability reductions conflict with the rearmament priority unless accepted only as a tactical deception or temporary expedient.

axes.brief: The sovereign racial state rejects superior international institutions and treats agreements instrumentally.
axes.counterEvidence: Cross-border ethnic claims and conquest go beyond defence of existing boundaries, but do not imply impartial internationalism or equal shared rule.

answers.rationale: The programme asserts strong central national authority rather than outside final lawmaking power.
International decisions opposed by leadership cannot legitimately override the national-racial state’s objectives.
Domestic political authority takes precedence over international court rulings that conflict with regime policy.
Alliances may advance expansion, but commitments have no independent authority overriding the regime’s strategic freedom.
Programme point 2 repudiates constraining treaties, supporting withdrawal without approval from external institutions.
Binding international adjudication against regime officials conflicts with the state’s unrestricted political authority.
Regime-defined national interests override objectives imposed by international institutions.
Environmental coordination cannot establish a superior international authority over the national state.
Foreign-policy independence is preferred, though tactical alliances are permissible when they advance the regime’s aims.
International human-rights demands cannot constrain laws founded on racial exclusion and dictatorship.
The autarkic economic strategy favours sovereign control of currency and foreign exchange.
Shared projects may be useful, but pooled authority has no claim against national strategic control.
Racial admission policy requires sole national control rather than shared authority at the border.
Trade agreements are acceptable instrumentally, while independent revision remains available for autarky and war preparation.
The sovereign Reich is not to be subordinated to an equal international political federation.
Enforcing collective rules is rejected when neutrality or unilateral action better serves immediate regime interests.

axes.brief: Private industrial ownership survives where it serves compulsory national objectives; the programme also calls for selected nationalisation and extensive state intervention.
axes.counterEvidence: State direction, racial expropriation and public ownership are distinct. The 1936 memorandum retains private firms while threatening replacement if they will not perform assigned tasks.

answers.rationale: The 1936 programme relies on private industry, and the 1928 clarification affirms private ownership, subject to political-racial conditions.
Utility networks may remain public or private provided the state controls their strategic functions; title is secondary to direction.
Comparable service outcomes do not settle ownership where political control and racial eligibility also determine the choice.
Programme point 13 and the memorandum permit public enterprise where strategic tasks are not delivered by private firms.
National health objectives prescribe state control and discriminatory priorities without one universal ownership form for healthcare facilities.
Integrated strategic rail infrastructure fits the programme’s strong central state and mobilisation requirements, inferred rather than a direct ownership clause.
Lower cost can favour contracting, but ownership selection also depends on regime control, labour and racial objectives.
Mixed private activity and state economic intervention permit public banks alongside private institutions serving the national plan.
Commercial assets may be sold if control survives, but blanket privatisation is not a governing principle of the memorandum.
Housing may serve population policy through public ownership or subsidised private provision; no doctrinal substantial public share is required.
The memorandum retains private industry when it performs state-assigned strategic tasks, supporting private security-relevant firms under effective control.
Resource extraction can be private or state-owned; assured wartime supply matters more than a universal ownership rule.
Routine services may be contracted, but private title is not inherently preferred over reliable state provision.
Strategic capacity can be retained or created publicly regardless of sale proceeds when required for rearmament.
Strategic production can require support despite losses, so repeated subsidy is insufficient by itself to justify sale.
Programme point 23’s comprehensive political control of communications supports a state national broadcaster rather than an exclusively private system.

axes.brief: Autarky, controlled imports and strategic substitution dominate the 1936 economic programme.
axes.counterEvidence: Foreign trade persists where it supplies essential inputs and serves war preparation. The regime’s objective is controlled dependence reduction, not the literal end of all exchange.

answers.rationale: Protective restrictions serve the regime’s requirement to secure domestic productive capacity.
Removing most barriers despite domestic losses conflicts with the 1936 programme of strategic economic control.
Domestic supply can be preferred despite higher cost to reduce exposure to foreign interruption.
Firms cannot freely select foreign sources when foreign-exchange and strategic supply priorities dictate otherwise.
The memorandum demands domestic substitutes for essential wartime materials despite cost disadvantages.
Unilateral tariff reductions are not a general obligation where national production and bargaining power are paramount.
New strategic industries can be protected until they deliver substitutes needed for military readiness.
Foreign investors cannot claim equal terms against political-racial control and economic independence requirements.
Domestic provisioning and food independence support agricultural import restrictions.
The state need not expose strategic producers to foreign competition when protection serves war preparation.
Retaliatory tariffs can be used as instruments of national economic pressure rather than restrained by free-trade principles.
Origin-neutral taxation may be convenient, but discrimination is permissible when it serves national supply and strategic priorities.
Foreign subsidies provide a reason to restrict imports threatening the regime’s chosen domestic producers.
Removing tariffs despite greater dependence conflicts with the autarkic programme’s explicit strategic aim.
Foreign control of strategic enterprises is incompatible with assured national command over war-relevant production.
Unrestricted foreign digital services would conflict with controlled trade and communications in this expressly modern analogy.

axes.brief: The 1936 memorandum directs production, investment and inputs toward rearmament while using private firms as executors.
axes.counterEvidence: Private title and managerial initiative are retained in places; they do not amount to freedom to reject compulsory strategic tasks.

answers.rationale: The memorandum requires firms to perform state-assigned tasks rather than decide production solely for themselves.
Compulsory targets for strategic materials are central to the four-year military preparation programme.
Prices remain subordinate to controls required for rearmament and national resource allocation.
Investment must follow the leadership’s national plan for military and economic readiness.
Consumer demand cannot determine closure or expansion when the national war plan requires different production.
Essential-price control is compatible with directing resources and limiting consumption for military priorities.
Entry into strategic production is subject to the state’s allocation priorities rather than an unconditional competitive right.
Directing credit is consistent with making financial resources serve the national rearmament programme.
Free capital movement conflicts with the memorandum’s control over scarce foreign exchange and imported resources.
Selected strategic substitutes receive support even when ordinary private profitability would discourage them.
Competing private money outside political control conflicts with central direction of national financial resources.
The regime can impose wage minima or other wage controls, but its central priority is labour mobilisation rather than a universal protective minimum.
Independent employer-worker bargaining cannot supersede nationally imposed labour and rearmament priorities.
Central-bank policy is subordinated to the financing and allocation needs of the national plan.
Unrestricted market rents can be limited when they conflict with population management and national economic mobilisation.
National production and distribution are coordinated beyond emergencies under the four-year programme.

axes.brief: Selective social provision serves the regime-defined racial community while hierarchy and war mobilisation remain central.
axes.counterEvidence: Programme profit-sharing and welfare rhetoric do not establish universal egalitarian redistribution; outsiders were dispossessed and excluded rather than treated as equal beneficiaries.

answers.rationale: Welfare and profit-sharing rhetoric permit some narrowing, while class hierarchy and war priorities reject equalisation as an overriding purpose.
Income gaps alone do not outweigh productive hierarchy when they serve the national-racial state.
Stronger support may advance population policy, but higher taxes for minimum incomes compete with military allocation priorities.
The programme exceeds bare destitution relief for favoured groups, yet does not commit benefits to substantially equalising all living standards.
Tax progressivity is an available instrument, not a central doctrinal requirement superior to war finance and productive incentives.
Favoured private owners and producers may retain unequal rewards, subject to state requisition and political control.
Family continuity can favour inheritance while revenue needs justify taxation; the programme does not prescribe redistribution through large-estate taxation.
Compulsory work and mobilisation favour restricting support for those deemed able to work, although benefits for favoured families can continue.
Wealth transfers can serve regime goals, but the doctrine’s expropriations are not equivalent to an impartial low-income wealth-tax programme.
Benefit levels follow demographic and military priorities rather than a consistent low-tax principle.
Old-age welfare and family supplements aim beyond immediate survival for recognised beneficiaries, without universal inclusion.
Neither tax cuts nor cash-benefit expansion consistently outranks the state’s changing racial and military objectives.
Family supplements demonstrate acceptance of income assistance to favoured working households rather than exclusive reliance on market pay.
Equal marginal tax rates have no doctrinal priority over selective state financing requirements.
Point 17’s land reform is qualified by private property and discriminatory expropriation; compensated egalitarian redistribution is not a clear general commitment.
Family supplements can reach households beyond bare destitution, although eligibility is racially and politically restricted.

axes.brief: The programme uses positive Christianity while making religious life subordinate to the racial state; the regime also pressures and persecutes dissenting churches.
axes.counterEvidence: This is neither clerical sovereignty nor consistent neutral secularism. Official Christian language and institutional accommodation coexist with anti-clerical factions and state supremacy.

answers.rationale: Racial state purposes dominate law, while official Christian rhetoric supplies selective religious justification; neither pure separation nor theology alone defines legitimacy.
Positive Christianity has official symbolic standing, but religious authorities do not determine the regime’s legal programme.
Church permission cannot bind political policy; the state represses religious opposition when it obstructs its aims.
The programme endorses positive Christianity without one binding denomination, while internal hostility prevents a consistent confessional constitutional model.
Religious instruction can be accommodated or reshaped, but neutral teaching is not a principle capable of constraining racial political education.
Faith cultivation can serve political accommodation, while hostile factions seek to weaken churches; neither a uniform confessional curriculum nor its total absence follows.
State courts serve civil-political authority rather than obeying independent church rulings as superior law.

Religious authorities have no general institutional entitlement to review proposed national laws; the regime subordinates church influence to political control even where it accommodates religious institutions.
Religious elements may appear at official occasions, while state ideology can replace them; an unconditional prohibition is not doctrinal.
Funds may support compliant religious institutions, but strengthening faith as such is subordinate to political-racial usefulness.
Christian symbols can be retained instrumentally, while regime symbolism predominates; neither compulsory removal nor universal endorsement is intrinsic.
Predominant Christian festivals can remain officially recognised within the programme’s selective Christian-national presentation.
Clerical office does not confer an automatic government seat against the regime’s political-racial selection rules.
Religious privileges can be accommodated, but the doctrine supplies no general independent exemption entitlement against fiscal and political state needs.
Independent religious approval cannot control state marriage policy, particularly where racial legislation dictates eligibility.
Binding autonomous religious family jurisdiction is disfavoured where it can conflict with racial marriage and state population policy.

axes.brief: The regime promotes sex-differentiated roles and racially selected reproduction while subordinating conventional family morality to population goals.
axes.counterEvidence: Lebensborn support for selected unmarried mothers and wartime mobilisation of women qualify a simple traditional-marriage-only portrayal. Modern identity terminology is assessed by analogy, not attributed as historical language.

answers.rationale: Changing personal values do not justify social transformation unless it serves the state’s racial-national project.
Conventional family roles are promoted, qualified by the regime’s willingness to depart from them for reproductive and military goals.
Marriage receives special recognition, although selected unmarried mothers can receive support when they serve racial population policy.
Official propaganda assigns women primary maternal and domestic responsibilities while men are oriented toward military-national duty.
The reproductive racial-family ideal does not support marriage equality for same-sex couples.
Marriage loans and family honours explicitly promote the married reproductive household as a preferred model.
For the favoured population, the regime increases penalties for abortion to promote births; coerced measures against excluded people are not reproductive autonomy.
Compulsory youth and school formation subordinates parental disagreement to state racial and sexual instruction.
The regime’s reproductive and persecutory sexual order conflicts with equal social acceptance of same-sex adoptive parents.
Gendered moral expectations guide public presentation, although national physical culture can modify particular conventional dress rules.
Self-defined identity has no independent authority to revise the regime’s fixed racial and sexual classifications.
State-approved inherited moral norms are transmitted, except where racial mobilisation requires the regime to replace them.
Wartime labour can require women in unconventional roles, but it does not establish equal social acceptance of voluntary departure from prescribed roles.
The regime’s radical transformation and coercive mobilisation reject gradualism when rapid change serves political objectives.
The state can teach about disapproved identities as part of indoctrination; merely descriptive coverage does not establish equal acceptance or a clear prohibition.
Ancestral symbolism is valued, but the regime discards customs when they obstruct population, military or political priorities.

axes.brief: Rearmament, synthetic substitutes and racial population engineering favour instrumental technological development.
axes.counterEvidence: This does not establish a historical position on every modern technology or imply that all environmental preservation disappeared. Modern biomedical analogies distinguish regime objectives from genuine safety evidence.

answers.rationale: Early benefits to military or productive capacity can justify deployment despite uncertainty, as reflected in urgent synthetic-substitute development.
A universal long-term trial requirement conflicts with the memorandum’s urgent timetable where strategic benefits demand rapid production.
Major infrastructure can override habitat preservation when it advances national mobilisation and expansion.
Favoured-population health matters, but urgency and coercive medical ideology can override caution; no consistent universal waiting rule follows.
Productivity-enhancing automation is favoured where it strengthens state capacity, with labour reassigned to national tasks.
Undisturbed habitat does not have a general veto over infrastructure needed for military and economic expansion.
Cultivated food is cautiously inferred as acceptable if it improves strategic provisioning, analogous to synthetic substitutes rather than a documented historical endorsement.
Enhancement useful to the state can encourage experimentation, while protecting favoured personnel can justify trials; a fixed long-term threshold is not prescribed.
Technical substitutes align with the regime’s drive for production, although consumption can also be restricted for state priorities.
Uncertain environmental effects would not generally override urgently prioritised national construction in the mobilisation programme.
Adult choice and basic safety alone cannot justify access to enhancement against state racial and strategic controls.
Reliable diagnosis can protect favoured populations, but the regime’s urgency and discriminatory medicine preclude inferring a universal across-group testing rule.
The ideology’s coercive hereditary-improvement project supports an analogy favouring controlled enhancement experiments, without treating its racial pseudoscience as valid.
A general long-term ecosystem-evidence requirement would be subordinate to strategic food-production priorities, rather than automatically blocking higher yields.
Housing and transport serving population and mobilisation goals can take priority over undeveloped land.
Potential irreversible harm does not categorically defeat projects leadership judges necessary for racial or military objectives.

axes.brief: The programme demands a strong central Reich with overriding authority over territorial institutions.
axes.counterEvidence: Regional administration can continue, but not as independently protected political authority capable of resisting the national leadership.

answers.rationale: Programme point 25 rejects protected regional resistance to the central Reich’s authority.
The central state holds final authority over disputes concerning regional powers.
Regional secession would fracture the unified Reich and is not a right conferred by local majorities.
A region cannot block a national programme merely because its policy has local electoral support.
Regional constitutional autonomy is inconsistent with the programme’s unlimited central authority over territorial organisations.
Integrated political policing requires central command rather than independently directed regional forces.
National mobilisation takes precedence over local retention of most tax resources.
Programme point 20 calls for national reconstruction of education to inculcate the state’s political conception.
Regional tax differences may be tolerated administratively but cannot constrain nationally directed finance and production.
Employment regulation follows national labour mobilisation rather than competing regional political preferences.
Local voters cannot independently redesign territorial authority against the central regime’s organisational requirements.
National racial-health and population objectives take precedence over regional healthcare-coverage preferences.
Autonomous Indigenous political institutions conflict with the regime’s hierarchical and centrally imposed racial territorial order.
Central direction can limit regional tax competition whenever it disrupts national economic allocation.
Even locally contained wildlife decisions remain subject to central political authority rather than a protected regional entitlement.
Cross-regional disaster response fits central mobilisation and overriding national command.

axes.brief: Nazi ideology falsely attributes broad human mental and behavioural characteristics to inherited racial essence. The profile records those assertions, not scientific facts.
axes.counterEvidence: The regime also used extensive education and propaganda. Such social conditioning does not erase its asserted hereditary hierarchy, but specific traits not covered by the doctrine remain conditional rather than fabricated biological findings.

answers.rationale: The ideology asserted inherited racial character as foundational, subordinating upbringing in its false hierarchy of human conduct.
Its pseudoscientific hierarchy attributed intellectual capacities to inherited racial identity, implying an inherited explanation of national-group differences.
The doctrine presented sex-differentiated reproductive and social roles as grounded in biology rather than mainly learned expectations.
Racial essentialism does not specify the comparative causes of individual stress sensitivity; training and embodied disposition both fit its model.
The ideology assigned inherited group character a major role in capacities and inclinations despite using education to shape approved interests.
Martial training and supposed inherited character both enter the doctrine; a specific general predominance claim for individual risk-taking is not established.
Cooperation was organised through propaganda, yet the ideology falsely treated racial membership as a prior basis of community capacity.
Its racial moral hierarchy is not a precise theory of individual empathy variation, so this narrower causal comparison is left substantively conditional.
Compulsory training assumes attention can be shaped, while hereditary ideology allows disposition; neither source specifies the relative causal primacy here.
The ideology’s claim that racial inheritance shapes moral character supports a biological leaning, recorded as its false essentialist assertion.
The regime invoked supposedly innate racial struggle and enemies, despite actively teaching threat narratives through propaganda.
Its broad hereditary account of character supports a biological leaning on temperament, without presenting that doctrine as empirical evidence.
Racially regulated partner selection and propaganda coexist; prescribing acceptable appearance does not establish the relative causes of aesthetic preferences.
The ideology falsely attributed threatening or criminal behaviour to inherited racial essence, a core pseudoscientific premise of its persecution.
Its asserted racial character hierarchy contradicts an account placing learned self-control above inherited racial tendencies.
Prescribed sex roles and state wage control complicate any market-value account; biological ideology alone does not prove its preferred explanation of the economic pay gap.

review.reviewer: Codex /root, separate evidence review of /root/libertarian_historical assessment
review.notes: Independently read all 240 answers against the exact bank and checked the NSDAP programme including its 1928 property clarification, the full 1936 autarky memorandum, and USHMM accounts of racism, women and churches. Added the 1935 citizenship law and implementing regulation to correct Democracy03: the question concerns citizens, so exclusion from citizenship is not by itself evidence for an education/intelligence voting restriction. Retained a mixed answer distinguishing formal selected-citizen voting from revocable political status and meaningful electoral accountability. Clarified that religious review is not identical to a veto. Checked all neutral-count warnings, preserving conditional ownership, fiscal, church and technology judgements. Racial behavioural assertions are expressly attributed to Nazi pseudoscience; narrow trait claims are not invented from the label. Private title is distinguished from compulsory economic direction, and selective welfare from universal provision. No similarity or desired score influenced corrections.
